messages.subject: Re: Question about fixed effects in polytomous models (with mixedmirt)
messages.subject_clean: Question about fixed effects in polytomous models (with mixedmirt)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Josh,

Your item here is actually

1 / (1+exp[-(1.015*theta + 4.937 -.201*groupM)]

so those in groupM actually have a lower overall intercept for this item (item is more difficult compared to the other group). You can interpret this as a kind of uniform DIF, though without scaling of the latent trait parameters I wouldn't necessarily interpret it as such.

The lr.fixed term is used to decompose theta into regression terms, in the same form as a latent regression model. So if you use this the decomposition will affect all items where theta affects the response, while fixed can be more isolated and only affect specific items in isolation. If you haven't yet, see the associated JEM paper which talks about both these fixed and lr.fixed effects (that paper focuses more on the former, but there are many papers regarding the latter). HTH.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: Likelihood Functions
messages.body_plain:
No, this is not possible. Multidimensional IRT models are fitted jointly, so isolating the individual factor contributions is not possible. This would be analogous to trying to isolate the IVs in a linear regression model with multiple predictor variables --- at best, you could get a partial representation in the system, but this largely what is meant by the slopes themselves (the slope parameters in IRT are of course no different). And because of the bounded nature in the expected values, E(y| θ​​, ψ​​), the behaviour of the expected values is always contingent upon the remainder of the values in the system.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
It sounds like you want to use the lr.random input to mixedmirt to create this random effects hierarchy for the ability terms. lr.random accepts formulas, so that's how you would specify each random cluster's structure.

lr.random = ~1|school

where the student information random effect is automatically included in the structure (IRT models always include these, because that's the point of a measurement model). See the last example in help(mixedmirt) demonstrating this type of two-level structure, as well as the associated paper in JEM. HTH.

Phil

library(mirt)

mod <- mirt(Science, 1)
IRTpar1 <- coef(mod, IRTpars=TRUE)[[1]]
p1 <- extract.item(mod, 1)

par<-as.numeric(IRTpar1)
names(par)<-c("a","b1","b2","b3")
est<-rep(TRUE,length(par))
Theta<-matrix(seq(-6, 6, by=.2))

p.grm.old<-function(par,Theta,ncat){
a<-par[1]

b<-par[-1]

intermediate<-matrix(1, nrow = nrow(Theta), ncol = ncat+1)
intermediate[,ncat+1]<-0
final<-matrix(0, nrow = nrow(Theta), ncol = ncat)
for (i in 2:ncat){
intermediate[,i]<-((exp(a*(Theta-b[[i-1]])))/(1+exp(a*(Theta-b[[i-1]]))))
}
for (j in ncat:1){
final[,j]<-intermediate[,j]-intermediate[,j+1]
}
final
}

# compare
p.grm.old(par, Theta, 4)
probtrace(p1, Theta)

GRMold<-createItem(name = "GRMold", par=par, est=est,P=p.grm.old)

fit.l.grmtest<-mirt(Science, 1, 'GRMold', customItems=list(GRMold=GRMold))

# roughly the same log-likelihood
anova(mod, fit.l.grmtest)

Phil

In general, does mirt provide the first and second derivatives of estimated parameter to a maximization routine or just use a existing maximization routine without providing derivative estimates?
Thanks for your help in advance!

> I am asking a programming question here. For confirmatory MIRT (e.g., multidimensional GPCM) and EM method, the population distribution parameters (e.g., the mean vector and sigma matrix of a multivariate normal distribution of population thetas)  need to be estimated.  In mirt, in the M (maximization) step  are all the first and second derivatives of the estimated parameter provided to the Newton-Raphson (NR) procedure? If so, could someone provide a reference for the derivatives of those population distribution parameters? Intuitively, you may update those parameters based on the posterior theta distribution in each iteration (e.g., the theta mean in an iteration  is just the mean of the posterior theta estimates of the previous iteration). However, I tried it and it did not work.
> In general, does mirt provide the first and second derivatives of estimated parameter to a maximization routine or just use a existing maximization routine without providing derivative estimates?

It depends on the algorithm used, and whether the latent trait components are freely estimated or not. The way you describe it works fine in the EM algorithm, but that's not what mirt does because the derivative information in the M-step is actually quite important from computing the ACOV matrix via the Oakes Identity approximation method. So in this case, the gradient and Hessian are computed from the MV normal distribution when this prior is assumed.

Phil
